planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving it room to spread as a flat, ground-hugging mat rather than training it upright.

directions: The sole species in its genus, Russian cypress is a true ground-hugging conifer from the Sikhote-Alin mountains of the Russian Far East, forming overlapping horizontal sprays of soft, scale-like foliage that lies flat against slopes, boulders, and raised beds. Bright green through the growing season, the foliage takes on a bronze-purple cast in cold weather, a seasonal shift that distinguishes it from the many prostrate junipers it is often compared to. It tolerates both full sun and considerable shade, handles poor rocky soil and drought once established, and spreads wide without climbing, making it useful for cascading over a wall or filling a large rock garden slope without overtopping neighboring alpines. Give it sharp drainage and avoid heavy, waterlogged clay, which is the main cause of dieback in an otherwise trouble-free and very long-lived plant.

common_name: St. Mary's Broom Miniature Blue Spruce

planting.note: Set out grafted plants in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, reserving a permanent, uncrowded spot since this true miniature adds only a fraction of an inch most years.

directions: Propagated from a witch's broom found on the species, this cultivar keeps the steely blue needle color of full-sized Colorado blue spruce but on an irregular, globe-to-conical dwarf frame that stays under knee height for decades. Its congested, slightly uneven branching gives each specimen an individual character more akin to a bonsai subject than a uniform nursery shape, and it is prized among collectors for true-miniature conifer gardens and trough plantings. Full sun keeps the blue coloration most intense and the habit densest, while deep shade thins the needles and dulls the color. Plant in well-drained soil and avoid heavy pruning, which is rarely needed given its glacial growth rate.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; this cultivar needs no candle-pinching or shearing to hold its naturally dense, rounded shape.

directions: One of the most widely grown dwarf conifers in rock garden and miniature collections, Smidtii forms an extremely dense, symmetrical globe of short, dark green needles packed so tightly that individual shoots are barely visible. Growth is very slow, typically a few inches a year, allowing it to hold a tidy globe shape without any trimming for many seasons. Like the full-sized Bosnian pine it tolerates alkaline soil, wind, drought, and urban pollution better than most dwarf pines, making it a reliable anchor plant for a sunny rock garden bed or large trough. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, and resist the urge to shear it, since its natural habit is tighter than anything pruning would achieve.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; its tiny mature footprint suits a trough, raised scree bed, or miniature conifer collection better than open garden ground.

directions: A true-miniature selection out of the Mitsch Nursery breeding lines, this mugo pine builds an exceptionally dense, rounded bun of short, dark green needles, reaching barely a foot across after many years in the ground. Its scale sets it apart from the many larger mugo cultivars sold for general landscape use, making it one of the few mugo selections genuinely suited to a trough or small rock garden pocket without eventually outgrowing the space. Candle growth is naturally short, so no pinching is needed to keep the habit tight. Give it full sun and lean, sharply drained soil, since mugo pines in general are intolerant of wet, heavy ground.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; avoid poorly ventilated, humid sites, since common juniper selections are prone to fungal blight in sticky summer weather.

directions: A Scandinavian selection of common juniper, Repanda forms a dense, flat mat of soft, needle-like foliage that lies close to the ground and spreads steadily without climbing over nearby plants, in contrast to the more mounded habit of 'Compressa'. Foliage is a rich medium green through the growing season and takes on bronze tones in cold winters. It roots as it spreads in loose soil, helping it knit together into a weed-smothering groundcover on banks, between stepping stones, or cascading over a wall. Plant in full sun with sharp drainage and good air movement, since common juniper cultivars in general are more susceptible to twig blight in hot, humid, poorly ventilated spots than most other junipers.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; its very slow, congested growth suits a trough, rock garden pocket, or foundation planting where a full-sized hinoki cypress would not fit.

directions: Among the oldest dwarf hinoki cypress selections still in cultivation, 'Nana' builds a dense, irregular mound of dark green, shell-shaped foliage sprays held on congested, tiered branching, a shape distinct from the more upright, lacy texture of 'Nana Gracilis'. Growth is extremely slow, often under two inches a year, which keeps it in scale with rock gardens and mixed dwarf conifer beds for decades without pruning. Give it reliably moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and some relief from the harshest afternoon sun in hot climates, since scorched foliage is slow to regrow at this cultivar's pace. It combines well with low alpine perennials and other miniature conifers in a trough or raised rock garden bed.

common_name: Franky Boy Dwarf Golden Oriental Arborvitae

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, where the gold foliage colors most intensely; this dwarf globe form suits a rock garden or small bed far better than full-sized oriental arborvitae.

directions: Franky Boy is a dwarf, globe-shaped selection of oriental arborvitae with flattened, vertically arranged sprays of foliage that emerge bright golden-yellow in spring and hold good color through summer before settling toward bronze-green in winter cold. Its compact, rounded outline needs no shearing to stay tidy, a contrast to the larger, more open oriental arborvitae cultivars grown as screening. Full sun brings out the strongest gold color, while shade pushes the foliage toward plain green. Plant in well-drained soil, since oriental arborvitae in general is less tolerant of wet feet than many other dwarf conifers, and avoid overly rich soil that can cause lanky, uneven growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing it to spread wider than it grows tall as its nest-like center fills in.

directions: Tompa is a dense, slow-growing dwarf Norway spruce in the bird's-nest group, building a low mound of congested branching with a shallow central depression similar in habit to the better-known 'Nidiformis' but staying somewhat smaller and tighter overall. Dark green needles are held densely along short shoots, giving the mound a fine, uniform texture without any shearing. It works well as a foreground anchor in a rock garden or mixed dwarf conifer bed, where its horizontal spread contrasts nicely with upright conical selections nearby. Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and give it room to widen for years before it needs any renewal pruning.

planting.note: Sow seed on the surface in fall or very early spring, since light aids germination, into a lean, gritty, sharply drained scree mix in full sun.

directions: The most culturally iconic of all alpine wildflowers, edelweiss forms a low rosette of narrow, felted, silver-white leaves from which short stems rise in summer bearing star-shaped clusters of woolly white bracts surrounding tiny true flowers. In its native European high mountains it grows in thin, rocky, lime-rich soil above the treeline, and garden success depends on recreating that lean, fast-draining environment rather than treating it as an ordinary border perennial. Full sun and sharp drainage keep the felted foliage from rotting, while rich or damp soil quickly shortens its life. It is short-lived but usually self-sows modestly in a well-suited scree or rock garden, keeping a colony going from year to year.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall for natural winter stratification, or set small divisions in spring, into a lean, gritty, sharply drained scree or tufa mix in full sun.

directions: Spring sandwort forms a tight, moss-like cushion of fine, needle-thin leaves native to rocky and often metal-contaminated soils across Europe, where it tolerates mineral conditions few other plants can survive. In cultivation it is far less fussy, needing only lean, sharply drained soil to form a dense mat studded with small white, five-petaled flowers held just above the foliage in late spring and early summer. Its diminutive scale and tolerance of poor, gravelly ground make it a useful filler between larger rock garden specimens, in wall crevices, or along the edge of a trough. Keep it in full sun and avoid rich, organic soil, which encourages lax growth and crowns out the tight cushion habit that makes the plant worth growing.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall into a lean, gritty, sharply drained scree or crevice mix in full sun; this Great Plains and Rocky Mountain native needs winter cold to flower reliably the following spring.

directions: One of the earliest wildflowers to bloom across the dry grasslands and foothills where it grows wild, Easter daisy produces its white to pale pink, yellow-centered daisy flowers almost at ground level, often before the tight rosette of narrow, hairy leaves has any visible stem at all. This near-stemless habit, combined with a long, deep taproot adapted to sparse, fast-draining soil, makes it extremely drought-tolerant but intolerant of damp, rich garden ground. In a rock garden, crevice planting, or trough, give it the leanest, most mineral soil available and full sun, mimicking the exposed, wind-scoured sites it favors in nature. Established plants are long-lived and need no division, flowering again from the same taproot each spring.

planting.note: Press loose offsets onto the surface of lean, sharply drained gravelly soil in full sun to light shade in spring or fall; offsets detach on their own and need only to be collected and set in place.

directions: Closely related to Sempervivum but botanically distinct, Jovibarba hirta belongs to the so-called rolling hen and chicks group, producing small, fringed, hairy-leaved rosettes that eventually detach from the mother plant on a very short stalk and roll a short distance before rooting in place, a propagation habit unlike any true sempervivum. Rosette color ranges from green to reddish bronze depending on sun exposure and season, and like its relatives it flowers and dies after several years while the surrounding offsets carry the colony forward. Grow it exactly as you would a hardy sempervivum, in lean, very well-drained gravelly soil in full sun to light shade, where it forms a loose, spreading patch useful for filling gaps between larger rock garden plants. Winter wet, not cold, is the main risk to the shallow-rooted rosettes.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall and leave exposed to winter cold outdoors, into a lean, sharply drained scree or tufa mix in full sun; crown rot in wet winter conditions is the main cause of loss.

directions: Native to high limestone screes of the Pyrenees and neighboring ranges, this compact cushion plant forms a tight hummock of tiny, blue-green, three-lobed leaves densely packed on congested rosettes. In spring it covers itself in small, four-petaled flowers in shades of pale lilac to soft pink with a faint, sweet fragrance, held just above the foliage on short stalks. It is considered a choice but manageable subject for scree beds, tufa, and troughs, needing scrupulous drainage and a lime-rich, mineral growing medium rather than ordinary garden soil. Full sun and a gravel top-dressing that keeps the crown dry through wet weather are the keys to keeping this cushion tight and long-lived rather than losing it to rot.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall, or set small divisions in spring, into a lean, gritty, sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun; overhead winter rain protection improves survival in humid climates.

directions: Native to mountain scree in the Balkans and Greece, this diminutive woodruff forms a dense, spreading mat of narrow, grey-green leaves so densely covered in fine white hairs that the whole plant reads silvery from a distance. In late spring and early summer it is covered in small, soft-pink, tubular flowers held just above the woolly foliage, a strong contrast of color and texture well suited to the front of a trough or raised scree bed. The dense hair covering that gives the foliage its silver cast also makes it vulnerable to rot if water sits on the leaves, so sharp drainage, a gravel mulch, and shelter from prolonged winter wet matter more than cold tolerance for this plant's survival. Full sun and lean, mineral soil keep growth tight and the foliage at its most silvery.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall onto a lean, sharply drained limestone scree or tufa mix in full sun and leave undisturbed; this is among the slowest and most exacting cushion plants grown by rock gardeners, best attempted by experienced growers in a raised, well-ventilated bed.

directions: Kelseya is the sole species in its genus, a Rocky Mountain endemic confined to dry limestone cliffs and rock faces in Montana, Wyoming, and nearby states, where it forms an extremely hard, dense cushion of tiny, silvery, overlapping leaves built up over many years. Small pink to white flowers appear directly on the cushion surface in spring, nestled among the foliage rather than raised on stems. It is grown almost exclusively by specialist rock gardeners because of its glacial growth rate and intolerance of anything but bone-dry, mineral, alkaline soil with perfect drainage and air movement around the crown. Overhead winter rain protection and a limestone scree or tufa planting are essentially required for it to persist outside its native cliff habitat.
